About Student Health and Well-being
Our Vision
Advancing holistic student well-being.
Our Mission
Campus Wellness aspires to collaborate at an individual, community and systems level to enhance student well-being. We provide both proactive and responsive care and support, tailored to the diverse needs of students.
Our Commitment
Waterloo’s commitment to students’ overall well-being is affirmed in three key principles that shape the robust network of resources, programs, initiatives, and services dedicated to their mental health and well-being, all of which adhere to the University’s Privacy and Consent Policy . This commitment is further supported in the University’s adoption of the Okanagan Charter .
Our Principles
We prioritize the holistic well-being of students, supporting their mental, physical, spiritual, and emotional health with a commitment to meet their diverse needs.

Employment statistics
To support you through the co-op recruitment process, we share regular updates on co-op employment outcomes. These statistics help you understand overall hiring trends across terms, faculties and programs.
As of May 1, 2026, you can find co-op employment statistics through the Co-op Data Hub. You’ll find clear, accessible summaries every two weeks.

Understanding the co-op employment rate
The co‑op employment rate shows the proportion of co‑op students who have secured approved employment at different points in the recruitment cycle.
We share this information to help you understand overall job search trends and how employment outcomes typically change over time. Our employment rate calculations follow industry and government standards.
How we calculate the employment rate
We calculate the employment rate by dividing the number of employed students by the total number of students participating in co-op recruitment.
Employed students include those:
Secured employment through the Full-Cycle Service or Employer-Student Direct job boards
Arranged their own job
Returning to a previous employer
Note: Students who make sequence or program plan changes, as well as those who participate in Waterloo Experience (WE) Accelerate are not included in the employment rate.

We're a co-op accredited institution
The University of Waterloo is a member of Co-operative Education and Work-Integrated Learning (CEWIL) Canada . In 1979, CEWIL established the Accreditation Council to regulate post-secondary co-operative education programs in Canada and to accredit those that meet specific criteria in an effort to ensure the quality of the co-operative education program. To date, the University of Waterloo has more than 120+ CEWIL Canada-accredited co-op programs across six faculties.

Why can't I see my exact employer ranking?
Employer rankings are generally treated as confidential hiring information and are not typically shared with candidates during recruitment processes. Showing ranking numbers could also create confusion because employers can assign the same ranking to multiple candidates. For example, an employer with several openings may rank many students as a 2 or 3, making it impossible to accurately predict the final outcome. Instead of focusing on ranking numbers, you should rank jobs based on your genuine preferences.

Why is the ‘minimum sums’ algorithm used instead of a ‘deferred acceptance’ algorithm?
In 2025, Co-operative and Experiential Education (CEE) worked with a Faculty of Math professor to independently review the WaterlooWorks matching process. The review examined several matching algorithms and analyzed six years of ranking data.
The review found that the minimum sums and deferred acceptance (also known as stable marriage) algorithms produced very similar results for students and employers. In most cases, the difference was only one or two matches, and there was no meaningful difference in the overall quality of student outcomes.

Based on these findings, CEE determined that the benefits of switching algorithms would be minimal and will continue using the minimum sums algorithm.
What happens in case of a tie?
If two possible matches have the same combined ranking score, WaterlooWorks uses a random tiebreaker to determine which match is considered first. The tiebreaker does not favour either students or employers.

Protecting yourself from job posting scams
When searching for jobs, it's important to protect yourself from potential job posting scams.
A growing scam trend targets students and new grads seeking employment, both on public job boards and university employment portals.
Though WaterlooWorks job postings are carefully reviewed by Co-operative and Experiential Education in an effort to verify their legitimacy, we can't always catch fraudulent information. Sometimes scammers will post jobs with real company names, websites and information, but use fraudulent email addresses to correspond with students (among other tactics). The same is true of public job boards, where postings are often less closely monitored.
No matter where you find a job posting, it’s important to use caution and sound judgement when responding to job postings, attending interviews and accepting offers from employers.

Job search expectations
Finding a co-op job takes time, effort and persistence. Consider dedicating the same amount of time to recruiting as you would for an academic course. Setting aside regular time each week for your job search can help you stay organized and manage timelines.
Every hiring process is a little different, but most opportunities involve submitting an application, participating in one or more interviews and waiting for the employer to make a decision. Many students apply for jobs while also interviewing for others at the same time. Not every application leads to a job, but each one helps you build skills and prepare for future opportunities.
Before you start, review important dates and work term requirements so you can stay on track for co-op credit. If you have questions at any stage of the process, your Co-op Advisor is here to help.

Be in good academic standing
Be enrolled in a full-time course load prior to the work term
Have earned at least one COOP course credit
Apply before your 4A term

Course planning and academic considerations

Work term forfeits for full time studies
To convert (forfeit) a work term to start a full-time course load (where you currently have a scheduled work term) you must agree to the following conditions:
CEE will have you on record as being on a scheduled work term for the term in question, though you will no longer be eligible for co-op credit for that term. This will count as one of the work term opportunities to which you are entitled.
Your minimum co-op work term requirements will not change due to this forfeit.
By deciding to forfeit a scheduled work term to take full-time courses, you are not typically permitted to reschedule the forfeited work term.
Standard tuition fees will apply.
Fees, enrolment and administrative responsibilities

Managing finances during a co-op work term can feel challenging, especially when you are balancing income, OSAP, rent and daily expenses. Waterloo offers financial resources to help you plan ahead, manage costs and access supports when needed.
Co-op work term and OSAP
If you receive Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP) funding, it is important to understand how your co-op work terms affect your funding and loan status. Students on co-op are considered 100 per cent courseload for full-time OSAP, which can help cover living expenses (and tuition too, if you’re enrolled in courses).

Continuation of Interest Free Status (CIFS)
Continuation of Interest Free Status (CIFS) lets you keep your existing OSAP loans interest‑free and delay repayment while you’re in full‑time studies or on a co‑op work term. Applying on time helps prevent interest from being added to your loans.
Emergency Loan Program
If you experience unexpected financial challenges during a study or co-op term, short-term emergency loans may be available. These loans are designed to help with essential expenses while you work toward a longer-term solution.
Financial support while working abroad
If you are planning a co-op work term outside Canada, there are scholarships, grants, financial aid and other funding opportunities that may be able to assist you.

Harassment and discrimination
Your safety and well-being matter. Under the Ontario Human Rights Code , employees, including co-op students, have the right to be free from harassment and discrimination in the workplace. These protections apply to you just as they would to any permanent, part-time or contract employee.
The University of Waterloo will support you in any workplace, regardless of location, understanding that laws and policies may vary across regions. If something doesn’t feel right, support is available to help you navigate your options.
Harassment
Harassment is unwelcome comments or behaviours that are known, or should reasonably be known, to be unwelcome and that create a negative work environment.
Examples of harassment include:
Unwanted physical contact
Suggestive remarks or leering
Offensive, degrading or inappropriate jokes
Vexatious (annoying or provoking) comments

Finding a place to live on your co-op work term
Accepting a co‑op job in a new location is an exciting chance to learn, grow and experience something new. While housing can be one of the more challenging parts of relocating, especially with costs and availability to consider, there are supports and resources available to help you navigate the process.
It’s helpful to start thinking about housing early, even as you begin your job search . Waterloo co-op students work across Ontario, Canada, and around the world! Being open to different work locations can expand your job opportunities. You can lean on your networks, including peers, family, and other co-op students along the way. Be sure to make use of the available resources to help secure a living situation that works for you.

When should I start looking?
For co-op students, housing timelines can feel tight. It's helpful to stay flexible and start exploring your options early. While many housing resources will encourage renters to start looking 6-8 months in advance, as a co-op student, you may not have that much time.
Rather than waiting until you have a job offer, try to build your awareness of housing throughout the entire recruiting process. Whether you’re browsing job postings, preparing applications, interviewing or accepting a role, this early research can help you feel more prepared and confident when opportunities come up. However, we strongly recommend that you only sign a lease after you’ve accepted a job offer.

Co-op job offer withdrawals
Accepting a co‑op job is a significant step in your co-op journey and represents a commitment between you and an employer. While most co‑op work terms move forward as expected, there are rare situations where plans change before a work term begins. When this happens, the situation generally falls into one of two categories:
Renege – you break a commitment to an accepted job offer
Rescind – an employer breaks a commitment to an accepted job offer
These scenarios are uncommon, but when they occur, there are academic and administrative implications. If they occur, our team is available to provide guidance and support. If you have extenuating circumstances, you can request an exception by submitting a Policy 70 petition .

You can only accept one job per term. Once you accept an offer, you're considered employed for that work term and must stop applying for other positions. Reneges can affect not only your own co‑op progression, but also employer trust and future opportunities for fellow Waterloo students.
What happens when you renege?
Reneging on a co‑op job affects more than just the individual work term. There are consequences to reneging that impact your work term record and academic transcript.

Are not eligible to earn co‑op credit for that work term.
Lose full‑time equivalent student status for that term. This can impact things like immigration status, funding (e.g., OSAP) and eligibility for certain work visas (e.g., J1 visas).

Accepting a co-op job is an exciting step in your co-op journey. Once you accept an offer, you are committed to that role and are considered employed for that term. At this point, stop applying and interviewing for other jobs. Your work term record in WaterlooWorks becomes the official record of your employment.
If you choose to break a commitment to an accepted job offer, the University considers it a renege and it will affect your work term record, transcript and student status. We also expect employers to honour their offers, and if an employer withdraws an offer or significantly changes it, this is considered a rescind.

Your employment agreement
Your employment agreement, or contract, outlines the terms of your co-op job and helps set clear expectations for both you and your employer.
Here’s what to know:
Your employment agreement is between you and your employer. The University of Waterloo and Co-operative and Experiential Education (CEE) are not part of this agreement.
You maintain full-time student status while you’re employed on a scheduled work term.
You are expected to follow the terms of your agreement and your employer’s workplace policies, including working the full length of your work term until the end day listed in the agreement.

Safety at work
Your safety while on a work term is a top priority. It’s important to know that you have rights and responsibilities for your safety, your actions and others affected by your actions. The University adheres to the Ontario Occupational Health and Safety Act (OHSA) and bases its principles around workplace health and safety on the OHSA.
The OHSA guarantees you three basic rights:
Knowledge: your employer must inform you about hazards in the workplace. Ask if you’re not sure if something is dangerous.
Participation: you have the right to make recommendations on health and safety issues.;
Refusal: you have the right to refuse any work if you believe it endangers yourself or others.
Your employer must ensure a safe working environment by:
Ensuring that you use the required equipment, protective devices and clothing.
Advising you of potential danger.

If you have safety concerns about your job or if an accident or “near miss” occurs while you are on a work term:
Report it to your supervisor immediately.
Always inform your Co-op Advisor of any safety concern, accident or near miss. They'll reach out within one business day to offer support and guidance as you work through the incident with your employer. At the same time, we'll work with your employer to gather information about the incident and will follow up with them to discuss your concerns.
If you’re asked to complete a work task that may risk your well-being and your employer does not support your right to refuse, please notify your Co-op Advisor immediately.

What is the co-op fee for?

What are traditional-style and suite-style residences?
Campus Housing offers two styles of residences: traditional-style and suite-style. Most first-year students live in traditional-style residences while some first-year and most upper-year and graduate students live in suite-style residences.
Not sure which style is ideal for your on-campus residence experience?  Learn more about each style or take our “what’s your residence style” quiz.

Traditional-style residence
Traditional-style residences are the classic dorm experience where you have a bed, desk, and closet in a single bedroom or shared with another student (double room). There are shared washrooms on the floor (usually single-gender), and meals are typically eaten in the on-site cafeteria.
Suite-style residence
Suite-style residences are apartments or townhouses with a single or double shared bedroom, and you share a kitchen, living area, and bathroom with 2-3 other students that you and your roommates are responsible for cleaning.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
Do I need to register/ sign up for International Orientation?
Yes, you will need to register for International Orientation. Keep an eye on your @uwaterloo.ca student email in August for more information on how to register.
Do I have to go to International Orientation and First Year Orientation?
We strongly encourage you to attend both International Orientation and First Year Orientation .

International Orientation and First Year Orientation?

International Orientation will get you set up for life in Canada with activities and sessions planned specifically for your needs. First Year Orientation will help you get connected with your faculty and the greater Waterloo campus. Both orientations have some once-in-a-lifetime events that you don't want to miss!
Do I have to pay for International Orientation?
No, there is no additional fee associated with International Orientation.
How do I know if I am eligible for International Orientation?
If you identify as an international student beginning your undergraduate studies at the University of Waterloo, then you're eligible for International Orientation. This includes students who:
Are Canadian citizens but spent most of their life outside of Canada
Completed high school in Canada but hold citizenship from another country

If I register for International Orientation, do I have to attend every event?

7 reasons why you should manage your time in university
In university, managing your time is knowing your priorities and making sure that the things on your schedule align with your priorities. Planning your activities involves strategy so that you can get the most out of your time. Still not convinced? Here are the top 7 reasons why you should manage your time regularly in university.
The Friendship Check-In
University is full of opportunities to meet people, but building meaningful friendships isn't always easy. You might know lots of people but only trust a few or find that some friendships have changed over time.
How to set goals in university
Do you have a list of things that you’d like to accomplish by the end of your term? Year? Course? Program?
Having a list of goals is a great way to stay motivated and reflect on what you want to get out of university.
